utterances.speaker: G
utterances.text: Good evening, Mayor Kate, City Council members. My name is Kate Anderson. I'm the welfare program manager at San Rafael Fire Department. And I'm honored to speak to all of you tonight and everybody else in the room about the fire hazard severity zone maps. Quite a mouthful that have been introduced by Cal Fire and will impact San Rafael. This is to introduce an ordinance and I'm going to give you a little bit of background so a few key points before we dive in. I want to cover what these maps are. Why do they matter to the city of San Rafael and then what is the city's role? Diving in big picture. These fire hazard severity maps have been mapped statewide by Cal Fire. They designate three different hazard levels throughout the state. Those are very high, high and moderate. And what you can see here is a lot of different colors. The red is very high, orange is high, and then the yellow is moderate. There's also some gaps. Those white areas that might be the lra, which is local responsibility area. That's what covers San Fell as a municipality. And then the other blank areas that you see are federal responsibility areas. That's where we see a lot of our national forests, not not covering San Rafael and our area down here. Brief history of why these maps came to be I'm going to start with where we are now in 2025. Why we're just seeing these maps in San Rafael is that Cal Fire has been mandated to map the high zones in addition to the very high zones that have previously been designated for local responsibility areas. This really started back in the 1980s when we were starting to have a lot more destructive fires that were coming into our communities. And the state found a need to identify these areas in state responsibility areas to get a handle on where hazards are and to start urban planning better. Through the 1980s, this really started to build steam. And then in 1991 we had the Oakland Hills Fire, very devastating. And that's when the very high zones were designated in local responsibility where there was a lot of damage and that hadn't been identified before. Moving about 35 years into the future to now, we're seeing these zones mapped in old SRA in all those three different categories. Here's what San Rafael's map looks like. As I mentioned, we don't have any very high zones. We hadn't before and we don't now. What we have primarily are the moderate zones and a little bit of that high in the area of the Terra Linda Sleepy Hollow Divide. And what you see here in the dashed line, that's the San Rafael city boundary. So I also wanted to illustrate how these maps are contiguous throughout the county as well. So hazard versus risk. This is a question that we get asked a lot about. I really want to reiterate that these Cal fire maps identify levels of fire hazard and not risk. Hazards are physical conditions on the ground that create the likelihood of a fire occurring and the expected fire behavior. And these maps are intended to last a long while, so over decades. So we can use them as a planning tool into, into the future. What they don't consider the short term modifications like fuel reduction projects, defensible space that homeowners might do and home hardening aspects that really get into the building code. Risk is more of the potential damage or an impact that a wildfire may cause under existing conditions that include a lot of the modifications that I just mentioned. I want to reiterate one more time. These hazard maps are not a structure loss model and they're not risk maps. They're hazards only. And insurance companies. And we get this question a lot. Insurance are looking at at risk models. And there's nothing in these Cal Fire maps that they don't already have access to. They have their own models. And so these aren't contributing directly to insurance impacts to our homeowners and our residents. What does take into account of risk are the wildland urban interface maps that we have. The city has adopted these. And the wideland urban interface really defines an area where human development meets wildland areas. So we do see a lot of this in Siener Fell. We have a lot of open spaces where there's a transition from our residential development into those areas. The fire hazard severity zone maps, as I mentioned multiple times, they're looking at hazards only. So we may have wildland urban interface overlapping those fire hazard maps, but we may not have WUI in the same area where there's multiple zone designations. It only occurs where there's development. So coming Back to that map of overlaid our wideland urban interface. That's that that dashed polygon that you see. And then the lime green is areas that we've done our own fuel reduction. So we've already identified where we find the, the most hazardous areas and that intersection of where it meets development. Cal Fire is a pretty complex and thorough model that I'm not going to dive into the specifics of right now. But they do take into a lot of factors including fire history in the area, the vegetation type, flame length. It does incorporate ember spread and ember models, as well as the topography of an area and climate. So what's the city's role in this? We didn't create these maps, but we can request changes which is an elevation in the designations or additional areas that we may think need to be including the maps. We have reviewed these maps and at this point no change is requested. And we've noted that the designations align with our wui, our wildlife number interface boundary and pretty well with the topography as we understand it. This is a pretty busy graphic. So I've highlighted what matters to San Rafael, what changes with these designations. We now have high zones in San Rafael and so the biggest thing that that impacts is residential resale inspections. That would add about 2,000 properties are now eligible for that. If you decide to sell your property. There's also the expansion of 7A building requirements. That's more. The home hardening elements extended from our wideland urban interface boundary that I just showed to now all of the high designation areas. And then our defensible space requirements are already citywide and this isn't impacted directly. We have made these maps available on our website and we've also promoted them and solicited comment at multiple community events events. We have received a few public comments that were focused on insurance coverage which is why we wanted to cover that and individual property designations. And our next action is to introduce the ordinance and May 19 have the option to adopt. We choose to move forward.

utterances.text: Greeting, Mayor Kate, members of the council again. So this item actually contemplates two separate ordinances, although related, as noted. The first is proposed Update to chapter 2.55 of the city's municipal code, which is the purchasing policy. And then a second item related to recommendations to amend Chapter 11.50 of the Municipal code, which is the public works contract policy. There's some background information in the staff report. I will essentially highlight the changes that are being proposed. The. And I would say both of these are coming to the council in the context of, number one, the need and desire to periodically review our policies, particularly financial policies. And procurement's a big part of that on more or less an annual basis. And also the current update and the timeline for bringing it to you with this meeting would be that if approved, the changes would be in effect essentially at the start of the new fiscal year, which is also the timeline we're working on to implement our new Tyler Muniz financial system. And so because the design and configuration of that includes ensuring that we've got internal controls consistent with the policies, this makes sense to look at at this time. The. I think the purchasing policy, I would say, was Last updated in 2018. The proposals for amendments that are before the council this evening are fairly limited in scope. The first one would be a recommendation to increase the city manager's current contract authority from the $75,000 level to $100,000 level. We can speak to the rationale for that recommendation. So concurrent with that recommendation, we would be increasing the the threshold from informal to formal bid with it from 75 to 100,000. So all formally awarded contract would still come to the city council for award. That's how that is structured in terms of a little more nuanced implementation. The other two other changes is ones that we've essentially already implemented administratively, but we would be codifying them with the ordinance, and that is to clarify that the application of the award authority applies how it applies to change orders so that we're looking at the cumulative amount of the original contract and the change order. So even small change orders it would bring, the new not to exceed amount over threshold would come to the council for approval. And also clarifying under the section in current policy that requires that there are available unencumbered budget appropriations, AKA funding available to award the contract, we're proposing language that clarifies for situations where we're awarding a multi year contract where the funding is awarded on an annual basis by the council with the budget that there's language in the policy and then in our standard contract templates to clarify that the out years of the contract is contingent on subsequent appropriations. So that's different than say a construction contract where we might have the funding all up front for a multi year contract as opposed to an annual janitorial contract or an annual tree maintenance contract. So we want to make sure that that contract isn't binding on the council, but the contract's contingent on the funding provided by the council through the annual budget process. That pretty much covers the purging policy. I would note that the recommendation to increase the city manager's authority from 75 to 1,000 to 100,000, kind of two, I think, complementary rationales. The first is that was last updated in 2018 and with the 28% CPI for the Bay Area, if it was just to be kept up with inflation, it's right about 96, $97,000. So kind of in the rounding, we've also revisited where city manager authority is with other cities in the area. And at least for those of our population size. I think the question was, and our complexity, there's not too many cities with the complexity of San Rafael, but this is actually in line, if not even on the low end of cities that have gone to 100, 125,000, $50,000 authority. I could add that the second ordinance that speaks specifically to the public works contract policy that was Last amended in 2023 essentially to conform to the bidding and contract provisions that are provided in the state's Uniform Public Works Contract Act. And that's what establishes the dollar thresholds. The only change that we're proposing this evening for the council to consider is number one, update the policy to state that the contract award authority under the city's policy, Council is delegating that to the city manager. The current language is that it goes to the public works director. So this is really kind of just a little bit of a language cleanup. Doesn't really have too much of a change in practice. But we're ensuring that city manager ultimately has the ultimate authority on these contracts. And then we're also adding to the public works contract policy the language about the requirement for available funding in place at the time of contract award with the clarification that for multi year contracts, particularly maintenance contracts that are awarded under that policy that those are contingent on ongoing budget appropriations provided through the annual budget process. Should the council act on this this evening it's back before the council for your second reading at the May 19 meeting takes effective as effective 30 days after that. And so it aligns nicely with the work we're doing to update these for next fiscal year. Take any questions.

utterances.text: Good evening, mayor and council members. I'm Marissa Sanchez, Human Resources Director. I'm here tonight to provide an update on the City of San Rafael's vacancy rates and to present our compliance with the new state legislation. Assembly Bill 2561. The purpose of this report is twofold. First, to provide you with an overview of current vacancy rates across city departments. And second, to fulfill our new obligation under this assembly bill to report on vacancies in a public forum at least once per fiscal year year. Assembly Bill 2561 was passed to increase transparency around local government staffing. It requires cities like ours to track and publicly report vacancy data. How many open positions we have, what we're doing to fill them, and how they impact public services. The broader goal is accountability, helping cities like San Rafael not only track disinformation, but also use it to improve hiring practices and service delivery. The legislation emphasizes the importance of being transparent with the public about staffing challenges and Impacts. As of March 31st of this year, the city's overall vacancy rate was approximately 8%. This reflects consistent effort by human resources and the hiring departments to actively fill positions. Importantly, no individual bargaining unit exceeded the 20% vacancy threshold that would trigger additional reporting requirements under the law. And you may remember as recent as last year, what our vacancy rate percentages look like just before the approval of our new MOUs. So it's just something to think about. They have gone down quite a bit. This table here breaks down vacancy rates by bargaining group. As of March 31, SEIU currently has the highest rate at 14%, but again, none are at or above the 20% trigger. Most groups have very low or no vacancies at all, which is wonderful. It's a positive sign of staffing stability here at the city. So we're very excited about that. To meet our recruitment goals, we've been actively, actively posting positions online and on social media to search. I'm sorry, online to search. To reach a wider audience, we've implemented new internal vacancy tracking systems, are reviewing the hard to fill roles, and continually refine our strategies to ensure that we attract diverse and qualified candidates. And while we've made good progress, we still face challenges. Retention is critical. We want to keep the staff we worked so hard to recruit for. Budget pressures and competition from other agencies, especially for roles in public safety and technical areas like engineering, continue to be hurdles. But even with these challenges, the city is optimistic about the future and remains focused on strengthening recruitment, expediting our hiring practices, and supporting staff to maintain the service levels that we so desperately need. Looking ahead, we're focusing on four strategic priorities. Increase in our outreach, continuing to monitor how vacancies affect services, improving the efficiency of our hiring process, and giving the human resources team the support and training they need to be successful in this endeavor. This report is for informational purposes only, so there's no direct fiscal impact. Our finance director will be happy. I'm not asking for any money at this time tonight. We're simply asking the council to receive this report in compliance with this assembly bill. We will continue to provide updates annually or more frequently if necessary to ensure transparency and accountability. So thank you for your time and attention and I will take any questions.
